comment: Single source of truth for the SPFN Mobile module graph. Canonical format: exactly one module object per line inside "modules". Consumed by tools/validate/validate.sh and tools/cocoapods-compat/generate-podspec.sh.
notes: schemaVersion 4 made a module one-Swift-platform-capable. `linux` is either ABSENT, which means the module builds on Linux, or the literal false, which means DECLARED ABSENT: this module has no Linux half at all. `social-apple` and `social-google` are the two — both are written against frameworks only Apple ships (AuthenticationServices; UIKit and AppKit), and a Linux half would have been an empty seam. The key is written only where it is false, because an `androidModule`-shaped "name or null" spelling has no name to carry: there is one Swift target either way.

SwiftPM cannot condition a TARGET on a platform, only a target's dependency edge, so `linux: false` is not something the manifest can state. What makes it true in the build is in the sources: every source and test file of such a module is guarded whole — the first line of code is `#if canImport(...)` on the framework that file is written against and the last is its `#endif` — so the target compiles to an empty module on Linux. validate.sh section 8 checks that guarding file by file, and checks the other direction too: a module WITHOUT the key may not import an Apple-only framework outside a `#if canImport(` guard. Package.swift carries a comment saying where the mechanism lives; the comment is not the source of truth, this file is.

The same three-state rule `androidModule` follows applies here, for the same reason. A reader must tell an absent key (builds on Linux) from `false` (declared absent) from a value it could not read, and a reader that treats the third as a skip reports a clean graph having read nothing. validate.sh buckets every module line into linux-capable or declared-absent and fails unless the two add up to the number of module lines; a line carrying `"linux":` followed by anything but `false` lands in neither bucket and fails as unread (docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PITFALLS.md P7).

`swift-crypto` is the second Swift external dependency and the first that is not trait-gated. CryptoKit is Apple's and ships with every platform this package supports; Linux has none, and swift-crypto is Apple's own port of the same API, so `SPFNCore`, `SPFNAuth` and `SPFNClient` swap an import (`#if canImport(CryptoKit)`) and nothing else. Every target edge to it carries `.when(platforms: [.linux])`, so an iOS or macOS build never links it. SwiftPM still RESOLVES a platform-conditional dependency everywhere, so the lockfile names it on macOS too; `Package.resolved` is untracked, which is why nothing about that resolution is committed. Its own transitive dependency, swift-asn1, is resolved but never declared here: this allowlist holds the manifest's DIRECT dependencies, which are the ones this repository chooses.

`ui` is the UI runtime vocabulary and it depends on core alone, on purpose. What it holds is four types an app screen needs before it holds any screen: `Loadable` (loading·ready·empty·error) for one read, `Busy` (idle·busy·error) for one write, `FlowRoute`/`Flow` for a stack of routes with a presented flag, and `FlowHost`, the one place a platform navigator is bound to that stack. `Loadable.error` and `Busy.error` carry the core error envelope, which is the whole reason for the edge; nothing here needs a transport, a session or a generated operation, so there is no edge to client, auth or generated, and an app that only renders state does not link them.

`externalDeps.swift` is empty for `ui` and that is not an omission. SwiftUI and Observation are frameworks the OS ships, the way CryptoKit is — SwiftPM resolves no package for them, so the allowlist this file holds `Package.swift` to has nothing to list. Android has no equivalent: Compose and Navigation 3 are Maven artifacts like any other, so every one of them is named here and the validator holds `android/spfn-ui/build.gradle.kts` to exactly this list. The two platforms are asymmetric in the manifest because they are asymmetric in fact.

`ui` carries no `linux` key, so it builds on Linux — `Loadable`, `Busy`, `FlowRoute` and `Flow` are ordinary Swift with no framework behind them, and their transition suite is the same suite macOS runs. `FlowHost.swift` is the one file guarded whole on `#if canImport(SwiftUI)`, which is what a Linux build reduces the module to nothing but its non-UI types by. Declaring `"linux": false` would have been the other reading of "SwiftUI is Apple-only", and it is the wrong one: validate.sh section 8 then requires EVERY file of the module to be guarded whole, which would have made the Flow transition table — the evidence for the Swift half of the Swift·Kotlin symmetry — compile to nothing on the only Swift host this repository's gate runs on. SwiftUI was added to that section's Apple-only framework list instead, so the guard on FlowHost.swift is enforced rather than merely present.

A module exists here only once it carries an implementation. The persistence/sync and hybrid modules were declared in the Step 1 scaffold, never implemented, and published as empty coordinates through 0.1.0-alpha.3; they were dropped from the train instead. Adding one back means adding it with behaviour.
Dependency edges are a Step 1 scaffold proposal derived from the layered design; they carry no implementation and may be revised in Step 2.

The client module gained edges to auth and generated with the session change set: a session assembles a clientProofV1 proof (auth) over a generated operation and its generated request type. The transport boundary inside the same module still depends on core alone.

schemaVersion 3 made a module one-platform-capable. `androidModule` is either an Android module name or the literal null, and null means DECLARED ABSENT: this module has no Android half at all. `social-apple` is the first — Apple ships no native sign-in SDK for Android, so the Android half would have been a nonce accessor and an empty seam, while everything an Android app actually needs (SpfnSocialNonce, appleRequestValue, enroll with provider "apple") lives in spfn-client and stays there. `androidDependsOn` and `externalDeps.android` are null on the same line for the same reason: there is nothing on that side to depend on anything.

Every reader must tell `null` apart from a key it could not read. The two are different events — the first is a declaration, the second is a broken parse — and a reader that treats both as "skip" reports a clean graph when it has read nothing at all. validate.sh buckets every module line into android-backed or declared-iOS-only and fails unless the two buckets add up to the number of module lines, which is what makes the skip narrow (docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PITFALLS.md P7).

schemaVersion 2 added two keys with the provider adapter modules. `swiftTrait` names the SwiftPM trait that switches a target's external dependency on, and is absent on every module that has none. `externalDeps` is the ALLOWLIST the validator holds each platform's manifests to: an external dependency that is not listed here fails, and a listed one that no manifest declares fails too.

Neither new key is a substring of another key in this file and neither appears twice on a module line, so a line-scoped extraction cannot read one where it meant the other (docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PITFALLS.md P5). `swiftTrait` and `swiftTarget` share a prefix on purpose-free grounds only: every reader matches the full quoted key name, never a prefix.

The Android names in `externalDeps` are version-catalogue aliases with dots replaced by hyphens: `libs.androidx.credentials.play.services.auth` is `androidx-credentials-play-services-auth`. The Swift names are the SwiftPM package identity, which is the last path component of the repository URL.
